question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Yes. At **Norfolk Southern**, the balanced-team model and emphasis on test-driven development did not prevent an early quality failure.

In early **2020**, Matt launched the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement, modernizing **Norfolk Southern’s** legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, as the pandemic shifted work to remote, the client reported rising defects. His team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership rather than defending the metrics. A bottom-up audit found that an engineer had been solutioning from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story and writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete while defects went undetected. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

He showed those gaps openly, rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories, and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team. They redid the code and test cases properly. He also introduced Samman-style coaching: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing engineers with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Defect rates dropped as story quality and test-first discipline took hold, and client confidence was restored through transparency and visible improvement. Matt’s stated lesson was that “metrics like test coverage mean nothing without the practice behind them,” and cultural transformation requires consistent coaching, not just process change.

answer_md:
🐾 This is a strong one.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with documentation.

His responsibility was to ensure a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He assumed the IAM configuration and environment boundaries were correct, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. He also had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root cause was insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His stated lesson was that these were assumptions he should have verified rather than inherited. IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work, from payment-engine delivery to client integration and cross-border workflow design.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed more than an out-of-box deployment of Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. Different payment types had distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements. Existing regional systems also had separate data models, client configurations, entitlements, and transaction histories that had to be consolidated without interrupting live payments.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended onshore/offshore team of **40+** across **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase**. He managed the build-vs-configure boundary, determining where WebSeries ended and bespoke engineering was required. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and government tax payment modules, alongside Message Authentication Code security, payment-type-specific entitlements, sanctions screening, and real-time global reporting. He also led payments data migration, introduced compliance dashboards, and owned production support during rollout.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+** countries. The migration completed **without disruption to live payment operations**, and the compliance dashboards became standard operational tooling.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform’s adoption lagged because SDKs were missing, documentation was fragmented, and clients had no sandbox. Matt co-created a developer portal with Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, use case-driven documentation, and a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. He introduced environment virtualization for earlier testing, used Lean Product and XP practices, and conducted a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch; the portal team delivered over **261 additional story points** beyond its commitment.

At **RBC**, Matt designed cross-border workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, including real-time FX integration, automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer, and batch processing. The work produced a complete implementation blueprint, while revised payment cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays and improved SLA compliance.

In the “permit to fail” work, teams experimented more freely, repeat errors declined, and delivery timelines shortened. question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In early **2020**, Matt launched the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement, modernizing **Norfolk Southern**’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, as the pandemic moved work online, the client reported rising defects. The team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns reached both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and shared the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete while defects went undetected. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Rather than treating it solely as an individual performance issue, Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team. They redid the code and test cases properly.

He used the Samman coaching approach: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, lunch and learns, and pairing engineers with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression. He also restructured agile ceremonies and provided product management and SMART story training.

Defect rates dropped as story quality and test-first discipline took hold. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and client and account leadership confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvement.

question: How long did that take?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built and ran that organization.

At **Accenture**, Matt scaled the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers to **150+ practitioners** across engineering, product, architecture, and design. The CIC stories identify a **10-person pilot**, rather than a **4-person** starting team. Many new hires lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience, and the organization was deliberately flat: managers did not sit on daily delivery teams. Matt had to build hiring, development, evaluation, and promotion processes without adding management layers.

He partnered with recruiting across **4 sourcing channels**: internal bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live scoping exercises. Interviewers recorded independent votes, and Matt held the closing interview and made the final decision on every offer. During scaling pushes, the process produced **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**, with interview participation capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** to protect delivery time.

New hires moved through tailored enablement and round-robin pairing with experienced practitioners. The learning model was “I do, we do, you do.” Matt established balanced teams combining product, engineering, and design, supported by mentors, skills matrices, peer-led tech talks, and retrospectives.

The organization operated through **11 to 13 direct-report practice and client leads**. Team anchors kept those leads informed about technical progress, team dynamics, and resource needs. Monday allocation reviews brought Matt and the leads together to assign practitioners across client engagements, training, and accelerator development. Performance feedback came from recent pairing partners, product managers, and anchors, rather than a manager’s impressions.

Over **4 years**, the organization reached **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**. CIC delivery achieved **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments, with **10-person balanced teams** delivering equivalent output to traditional **20-person teams**.

🐾 Here’s how the two engagements compare.

Both involved Execution & Delivery, with different starting points: **Fiserv** was a recovery of a troubled card portal, including Org & Working-Model Transformation. **JP Morgan Chase** ACCESS was custom payment engineering and legacy consolidation, including Risk & Responsible Tech.

At **Fiserv**, Matt took over roughly **7 months** into an **\$8.5M** initiative. The **45-person** team had missed consecutive deadlines, stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation, and **3 external vendors** had uncoordinated dependencies. SVN tree conflicts halted builds, requirements lived in **200-page** BRDs, and releases followed a **6-month** waterfall cycle. At **JP Morgan Chase**, the challenge was different: Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform could not supply the payment modules, security controls, and approval workflows required for **135,**000+ client**s** across **180+ countries**.

Matt’s **Fiserv** work changed how the team defined, built, and released work. He decomposed requirements into persona-based user stories, tracked **47 acceptance criteria** as JIRA Epics, introduced **2-week** sprints and biweekly demos, and established follow-the-sun handoffs. Instead of retaining static Word documents for compliance, he used JIRA audit trails and attached ADA scans. He replaced SVN with Git, required senior-developer reviews and unit tests, and introduced Maven, Artifactory, Hudson, SonarQube, and JUnit quality gates.

For ACCESS, Matt managed a **40+** blended team and spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices. Rather than treating WebSeries as an out-of-box deployment, he managed the build-versus-configure boundary: delivering bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax-payment capabilities, MAC security, and payment-type-specific RBAC. Bulk permission changes replaced per-user configuration. He also delivered a payments gateway across **12 countries** and led legacy data migration with compliance dashboards and production validation.

**Fiserv** finished **3% under budget**, met **47/47 acceptance criteria**, launched with **zero critical defects**, and avoided **\$500K in penalties**. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; entitlement management fell from days to minutes, and regional payment data was consolidated without disruption to live payment operations.

answer_md:
🐾 Found it! Matt was brought in roughly seven months into **Fiserv**'s 14-month, **$8.5M** white-label card portal program, the shared platform behind branded credit card sites for **2M+** cardholders across **15** financial institutions. The **45-person** globally dispersed team had missed multiple consecutive deadlines, and client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. He recovered a Q4 release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **$500K** in penalties, and the program was delivered **3%** under budget with zero critical defects at launch.

Want to hear how he moved that team from 6-month waterfall releases to 2-week sprints?

🐾 Here's a great example.

At **Fiserv**, the **45-person** globally dispersed team was working with **6-month** release cycles and requirements buried in a **200-page** BRD organized by system modules. Developers were in India, testers in the Philippines, and designers in Ireland. The team had no visibility into work status, deadlines had been missed repeatedly, and stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. PMO and compliance also resisted moving to agile.

Matt replaced the single To Do/Done JIRA board with a multi-tiered Kanban/Scrum architecture, tracking the **47** acceptance criteria as Epics. He decomposed the BRD into persona-based user stories instead of system-module requirements. To coordinate work across time zones, he established a **7 AM CST** scrum-of-scrums for offshore-to-onshore handoffs and **11 PM CST** syncs for onshore-to-offshore handoffs.

He introduced bi-weekly sprint demos for stakeholder sign-off on branding, UI, and ADA compliance, rather than discovering issues at month **6**. When stakeholders lacked bandwidth for frequent feedback, he negotiated dedicated review windows. He retained existing steering committee reporting while adding sprint-level visibility.

For compliance, Matt used JIRA as the system of record, with audit trails, attached ADA scans, and developer comments instead of static Word documents. He coached offshore teams on empowerment over command-and-control and built JAWS/NVDA screen reader audits into the Definition of Done. Alongside that work, he introduced mandatory senior-developer code reviews, unit tests, and automated build quality gates.

The team moved to **2-week** sprints within **3 months**. JIRA provided real-time visibility to **50+** stakeholders across **3** time zones and satisfied PMO and compliance audit requirements. Separately, production deployment frequency increased from less than once per month to weekly-to-monthly cycles.

🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s **Norfolk Southern** work.

As a Director at **Accenture**, Matt led the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement: modernizing **Norfolk Southern’s** Revenue and Shipment Planning platform without stopping the railroad. Its mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. The client organization was shaped around mainframe thinking, account leadership expected waterfall delivery, and Matt’s team was learning a new working model as COVID forced remote work.

Matt brought cross-workstream representatives into event storming and domain-driven design sessions to map business functions, data flows, and dependencies. Rather than a wholesale replacement, the mainframe remained the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB rose beside it. Change data capture, API gateways, anti-corruption layers, and reconciliation supported incremental migration. Docker, Kubernetes, and automated CI/CD supported the new services; SNAP-E documentation captured APIs, dependencies, and risks.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System UI. They worked from personas through high-fidelity prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations, anchored on OKRs and data capture fidelity.

He also confronted a quality crisis rather than defending near-complete test coverage. An audit uncovered tests written after code and vague backlog stories. Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories, brought in frontend and backend TDD experts, and used boot camps, coding katas, and pairing.

Alongside delivery, he led a **2-day** CIC Academy course twice a month over **6 months**. Pairing met resistance: “I’m not paying for two people to do the work of one.” He let the client experience it firsthand and rotated scarce domain knowledge through teams using “I do, we do, you do.”

question: Tell me about his Norfolk Southern work.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what Matt worked on at **RBC**.

As a Senior Technology Architecture Manager at **Accenture**, Matt worked on **RBC’s** Day**2Day** Corporate Banking modernization, which was evaluating Bottomline WebSeries as the payment hub engine to replace the aging **RBC** Express portal. Existing systems had performance and scalability limitations and lacked digital offerings. Leadership needed an assessment of whether WebSeries could meet business requirements before committing further investment.

Matt conducted a structured architecture assessment across Data, Application, Technology, and Business Architecture. He combined code reviews, stakeholder interviews, and documentation analysis with direct experience implementing WebSeries on a prior payments program. Rather than assuming the proposed platform was the answer, he created architectural heat maps showing where its capabilities fell short, developed target-system models, and presented transparent cost-to-fix versus benefit comparisons. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the modularity required for **RBC’s** long-term digital operating model. **RBC** avoided investing further in that platform path and redirected technical resources toward higher-priority initiatives.

He also established the program’s PMO during discovery and requirements. Beyond status reporting, he created designated points of contact, a shared platform for real-time updates and daily summaries, and a task-tracking matrix to clarify assignments and prevent duplicate work. He maintained the roadmap, dependencies, budget, schedule, and risk framework across **RBC**, **Accenture**, and Bottomline Technologies. Centralized communication eliminated missed program updates, while reporting enabled faster issue resolution.

When the previous data conversion lead left early in the initiative, Matt took over that workstream from scratch. He analyzed legacy payment records, documented source-to-target transformation rules, planned mock conversion “dress rehearsals,” and established reconciliation checks for payment amounts and beneficiary details. He delivered the end-to-end conversion plan and coordinated onshore and offshore data scrubbing and validation teams.

Matt also owned engagement margin, staffing senior specialists early for architecture work and transitioning repeatable work to offshore and nearshore teams as the backlog matured.
